name: Mordent-Hollow
geological_features: Enormous lava tubes creating a hollow subsurface network
Surface punctuated by skylights into the tube system below
Ancient volcanic plains with preserved flow textures
specific_features: The Hollow Core — a lava tube network so extensive that the planet's interior is largely empty space
Skylights hundreds of meters across opening into caverns kilometers wide
resources: Protected subsurface volume ideal for habitat construction
Trace mineral deposits along tube walls
description: Mordent-Hollow is a medium-sized barren world that is, quite literally, mostly empty. Ancient volcanic activity created a lava tube network of such extraordinary extent that the planet's subsurface is more void than solid. Skylights — collapse points in the tube ceilings — dot the surface, opening into caverns of staggering scale. The largest tubes are kilometers in diameter and stretch for hundreds of kilometers without interruption.

The airless surface is a dark basaltic plain, unremarkable save for the regular occurrence of the skylights. Looking down through one of these openings is like peering into an underworld — the caverns below are pitch-black, enormous, and eerily empty. The temperature on the surface swings wildly between day and night, but inside the tubes it remains constant — cold but stable, shielded from radiation and micrometeorites.

The tube network has made Mordent-Hollow one of the most promising locations for large-scale habitat construction in the sector. The caverns provide ready-made enclosed volumes that need only to be sealed and pressurized, saving enormous time and expense compared to surface construction. Several pilot projects have successfully established pressurized sections of the tube network, and the results have exceeded expectations.

The planet's transformation from barren rock to potential population center is underway, with development corporations competing for rights to the most favorable tube sections. The hollow structure raises structural concerns — the planet's reduced mass makes its gravitational field weaker than its size suggests, and there are questions about long-term stability if the tubes are pressurized. Engineering surveys continue, but the economic momentum behind development may outpace the science meant to ensure its safety.
